key_insight: VLMs often produce illusion-appropriate answers by recalling memorized associations rather than perceiving visual changes — they persist with the same responses even when illusion cues are inverted, unlike humans.
problem_solved: Determines whether VLM outputs reflect genuine visual perception or pattern recall, and provides a systematic probing protocol to diagnose non-perceptual behavior on classic visual illusions.
method: Build a controlled benchmark of classic visual illusions paired with inverted/altered variants that flip the perceptual effect while keeping surface statistics similar.
Query VLMs (with standardized prompts) on original vs inverted images and quantify response consistency, agreement with human perception, and failure modes.
Analyze contributing factors (prompting, model architecture, training data artifacts) to separate perception-like responses from memorized pattern recall.
impact: Gives practitioners a practical evaluation to detect when VLMs rely on memorized templates rather than visual reasoning, informing model selection, fine-tuning, and dataset curation to improve real visual understanding.
visual_elements: Side-by-side image pairs: original illusion vs inverted variant with human answer vs VLM answer labels
Bar chart: percent of VLM responses that flip vs remain same across inversion conditions (compared to human flip rate)
Pipeline diagram: benchmark creation → standardized prompting → response analysis → attribution of causes
Heatmap/overlay: example saliency or attention map showing where model focuses versus human-relevant cues
paper_title: Do VLMs Perceive or Recall? Probing Visual Perception vs. Memory with Classic Visual Illusions
paper_authors: Xiaoxiao Sun, Mingyang Li, Kun yuan, Min Woo Sun, Mark Endo
